title: What Is Going On Right Now

lessons.title: कर रहा हूँ (kar rahā hū̃) — one word slid into the middle
lessons.gloss: I am doing, right now — three words, and the middle one is the only new thing

segments.text: Say I do — the habit. Now try to say what you are doing at this moment, and notice the habit form does not quite mean it.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: कर रहा हूँ

segments.text: कर रहा हूँ (kar rahā hū̃) — "I am doing," right now, said by a man.
Three words: the bare stem, then रहा, then the copula you have had since your third chapter.

utterances: piece: कर. what it carries: the action, bare.
piece: रहा. what it carries: that it is in progress.
piece: हूँ. what it carries: who, and that it is now.

segments.text: रहा is the past participle of रहना, "to stay, to remain." So the sentence says, almost literally, doing — having stayed — I am. The action is pictured as one you are still inside.
English does the same thing from a different angle: I am doing uses a participle too, and I remain at work is the same metaphor spelled out.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the stem is bare, and that is the point

segments.text: Look at what happens to the verb in each tense:

utterances: what you say: I do (habit). the verb: करता.
what you say: I am doing (now). the verb: कर.

segments.text: The habit puts an ending on the stem. The continuous takes the ending off and puts a separate word after it instead. Nothing else in the sentence moves.
That means the pattern works on any verb you know. Take the stem, add रहा, keep the copula: बोल रहा हूँ, जा रहा हूँ, खा रहा हूँ.

lessons.title: कर रही हूँ (kar rahī hū̃) — which of the three words listens
lessons.gloss: I am doing, said by a woman — the middle word bends and the other two do not

segments.text: रहा ends in -आ. Before reading on, guess what it does when a woman is speaking, and guess which of the other two words joins in.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: कर रही हूँ

segments.text: कर रही हूँ (kar rahī hū̃) — "I am doing," said by a woman.
One letter has changed, and it is in the middle word.

utterances: speaker: a man. the three words: कर रहा हूँ (kar rahā hū̃).
speaker: a woman. the three words: कर रही हूँ (kar rahī hū̃).

segments.text: The stem stays bare either way. The copula हूँ is about who is speaking rather than about gender, so it does not move. Only रहा bends, and it bends the way every -आ word you have met bends.
That is the tidiest arrangement you have seen yet: one word per job, and only the one that describes the action listens to gender.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the same ending, a fourth time

utterances: masculine: काला. feminine: काली.
masculine: बोलता. feminine: बोलती.
masculine: था. feminine: थी.
masculine: रहा. feminine: रही.

segments.text: Four places, one alternation. Every time a Hindi word ends in -आ and describes somebody, -ई is what it becomes for a woman — and by now you should expect it before you are told.

segments.text: Which of the three words bends? (The middle one, रहा / रही.) Why does the copula stay put? (It is about who, not about gender.) What is the fourth pair on the list? (रहा / रही.)

lessons.title: कर रहा है (kar rahā hai) — two words doing two different jobs
lessons.gloss: he is doing, she is doing — the last word changes for who, the middle one for what they are

segments.text: Say I am doing. Now point at somebody else and change only what has to change.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: कर रहा है

segments.text: वह कर रहा है (kar rahā hai)। — He is doing (it). वह कर रही है। — She is doing (it).
Only the last word moved when the subject changed from I to he:

utterances: subject: मैं. middle: रहा / रही. last: हूँ.
subject: वह. middle: रहा / रही. last: है.

segments.text: Two independent dials. The middle word answers what is the subject like and the last word answers which person is it. Turning one does nothing to the other, which is why you can build any combination without a table to memorise.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: it works on things as well as people

utterances: वह जा रहा है। means He is going.
वह आ रही है। means She is coming.

segments.text: A noun that is not a person still has a gender, and the middle word follows the noun rather than any person. That is how the weather sentence you learned long ago was put together — the rain is feminine, so the middle word ended in -ई — and the review lesson takes it apart.

lessons.title: कर रहे हैं (kar rahe haiṁ) — both dials turned to plural
lessons.gloss: we are doing, they are doing, and the form आप takes — the plural, in both dials at once

segments.text: You have two dials: the middle word and the last. Say the pronoun for we, and guess what a group does to each dial.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: कर रहे हैं

segments.text: हम कर रहे हैं। — We are doing (it). आप क्या कर रहे हैं? (āp kyā kar rahe haiṁ?) — What are you doing?
This time both words move:

utterances: subject: मैं. middle: रहा. last: हूँ.
subject: वह. middle: रहा. last: है.
subject: हम, वे, आप. middle: रहे. last: हैं.

segments.text: रहे is the plural of the same -आ / -ई / -ए set. हैं is the plural copula. Nothing here is new — it is the two dials you already have, both turned one notch.
At the तुम level the last word is हो: तुम क्या कर रहे हो?

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the question a listening paper asks

utterances: level: आप. the question: आप क्या कर रहे हैं? (āp kyā kar rahe haiṁ?)
level: तुम. the question: तुम क्या कर रहे हो?

segments.text: What are you doing? is one of the commonest openings in spoken Hindi, and the whole difference between the two rows is the last word. That is the level decision again, settling one more system.

lessons.title: do vartamān — the habit and the moment
lessons.gloss: what I do against what I am doing — the distinction English keeps and most languages do not

segments.text: Say both forms of to do that you now have — the habit and the one in progress — and try to say in English what separates them.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the pair

utterances: मैं हिंदी बोलता हूँ। means I speak Hindi.
मैं हिंदी बोल रहा हूँ। means I am speaking Hindi.

segments.text: The first is a fact about you. The second is a report about this minute.

This distinction is worth pausing on, because English speakers have it and most European learners of Hindi do not. French, German and Spanish all translate both of those lines with a single present tense; Hindi and English each keep two.

So the good news is that your instinct is already right. Where English says I am doing, Hindi says कर रहा हूँ (kar rahā hū̃). Where English says I do, Hindi says करता हूँ. Translate the shape, not the words.

One caution. Hindi leans on the habit form in a place English does not: for something happening in the near future that is already arranged, Hindi is happy with the habitual, where English reaches for I am.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: which word in the sentence tells you

utterances: form: habit. the shape of the verb: stem + -ता, then the copula.
form: in progress. the shape of the verb: bare stem, then रहा, then the copula.

segments.text: The copula is in both, so it tells you nothing. What decides it is whether the stem carries -ता or stands bare with रहा behind it.
अभी — the word for right now — sits comfortably with the second and strangely with the first, which is the quickest way to hear the difference.

segments.text: Name the three pieces of a continuous sentence, and say which two of them move, before you look at the table.

utterances: subject: मैं (m). middle and last: रहा हूँ.
subject: मैं (f). middle and last: रही हूँ.
subject: वह (m). middle and last: रहा है.
subject: वह (f). middle and last: रही है.
subject: हम, वे, आप. middle and last: रहे हैं.
subject: तुम. middle and last: रहे हो.

segments.text: The stem in front of all of them is bare, every time. Six rows and not one of them touches the verb.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two sentences that were built this way all along

segments.text: You have been saying this pattern for a long time without being given it:

utterances: sentence: एक बज रहा है. what it is: baj- bare, रहा, है.
sentence: बारिश हो रही है. what it is: ho- bare, रही, है.

segments.text: Neither was a lump. The clock one is masculine and the rain one is feminine, which is the only difference between them, and it is the middle word that shows it — exactly as the grid above says it should.

form: in progress. the verb: बोल रहा हूँ.
form: earlier habit. the verb: बोलता था.

segments.text: Three tenses off one stem, and the only thing you have to look at is what sits immediately after it.

lessons.title: आप क्या कर रहे हैं? (āp kyā kar rahe haiṁ?) — the question, and four ways to answer it
lessons.gloss: what are you doing? — the commonest opening in spoken Hindi, and answering it about yourself

segments.text: You have क्या for what. Put it in front of the plural continuous and you have the question this lesson is about.
— आप क्या कर रहे हैं? (āp kyā kar rahe haiṁ?) — मैं हिंदी बोल रहा हूँ।.

Three things are at work. क्या asks. रहे हैं is the plural because the question is to somebody addressed as आप. The answer drops back to रहा हूँ, because the answer is about one man speaking for himself — a woman answers बोल रही हूँ, and the question does not change, because the asker does not know yet who will answer.
Answer it four ways, out loud:
you are speaking Hindi.
you are going home.
you are eating.
and then say what you do in general, rather than now.
The fourth one is the trap and the test. What are you doing? takes the continuous; what do you do? takes the habit, and the two questions sound nearly the same in English.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: what a listening paper does with this

utterances: what you hear: ...रहा है. what it tells you: one man, right now.
what you hear: ...रही है. what it tells you: one woman, right now.
what you hear: ...रहे हैं. what it tells you: more than one, or आप.

segments.text: The middle word is doing almost all the work, and it sits at the end of the sentence where a listener hears it last. Train the ear on those three shapes and a personal-account listening item becomes three decisions instead of one guess.
